## Appendix A Notations and Conventions

Our results rely on numerous notational conventions and terminologies. For completeness, let us briefly summarize our nomenclature here.

#### Manifold and Index Conventions

Throughout our paper, the symbol ${\mathcal{M}}$ denotes the full four-dimensional manifold of spacetime. Within it resides zero-, one-, two-, and three-dimensional submanifolds, which we denote by ${\mathcal{P}}$ , ${\mathcal{C}}$ , ${\mathcal{S}}$ , and ${\mathcal{V}}$ , respectively. We often define ${\mathcal{S}}$ to be exact, so it is the boundary of a corresponding coboundary manifold ${\mathcal{V}}$ such that ${\mathcal{S}}=\partial{\mathcal{V}}$ . On the other hand, we take ${\mathcal{C}}$ to be closed, so it has no boundary and thus $\partial{\mathcal{C}}=0$ . In the Hamiltonian formalism, we perform a $3{\,+\,}1$ decomposition which generates quantities associated with a spatial three-dimensional submanifold ${\mathcal{M}}_{3}$ , like the three-dimensional intersection number $\Intersect_{3}$ .

Spacetime indices are $\mu,\nu,\rho,\sigma,\ldots\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ , while spatial indices are $i,j,k,l,\ldots\in\{1,2,3\}$ . Adjoint indices of the Lorentz group are $a,b,c,d,\ldots\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ while vector indices are $A,B,C,D,\cdots\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ . Undotted and dotted spinor indices are $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\ldots\in\{0,1\}$ and ${\dot{\alpha}},{\dot{\beta}},{\dot{\gamma}},{\dot{\delta}},\ldots\in\{0,1\}$ , respectively.

All epsilon tensors $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ and $\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ are pure permutation symbols valued in $\{+1,-1,0\}$ , sans dressing by metric-dependent determinant factors, so their indices are never partially raised or lowered. In particular, we employ the sign and normalization conventions,

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon^{1234}=+1\,,\quad dx^{\mu}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}dx^{\nu}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}dx^{\rho}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}dx^{\sigma}=\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hskip 1.00006ptd^{4}x\,,\quad\epsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=+4!\,. $$

On the other hand, $\epsilon^{ABCD}$ and $\epsilon_{ABCD}$ have Lorentz vector indices which are raised and lowered by the flat Euclidean metric $\delta_{AB}=\diag(+1,+1,+1,+1)$ .

#### Lorentz Algebra Conventions

Let us now summarize our conventions for the Lorentz Lie algebra. First of all, we employ an anti-Hermitian convention for Lie algebra generators $t_{a}$ so that $[t_{a},t_{b}]=f^{c}{}_{ab}\hskip 1.00006ptt_{c}$ without the imaginary unit. The adjoint and coadjoint actions on Lie algebra elements and their duals act as $(t_{a})^{i}{}_{j}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}\mapsto(\Omega^{-1})^{i}{}_{k}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{k}{}_{l}\hskip 1.00006pt\Omega^{l}{}_{j}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}$ and $Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})^{i}{}_{j}\mapsto Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(\Omega^{-1})^{i}{}_{k}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})^{k}{}_{l}\hskip 1.00006pt\Omega^{l}{}_{j}$ , respectively, so that $Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}\propto Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a}\hskip 0.24994ptt_{b})^{i}{}_{i}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{b}$ is invariant. In the main text, we have simply denoted these as $X^{a}\mapsto({\Omega}^{-1}\hskip-0.24994pt{X}\hskip 1.00006pt{\Omega})^{a}$ and $Y_{a}\mapsto({\Omega}^{-1}\hskip-0.24994pt{Y}\hskip 1.00006pt{\Omega})_{a}$ .

The generators of the Lorentz Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ are six anti-symmetric matrices $(t_{a})^{AB}=(t_{a})^{[AB]}$ , while those of the dual Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4)^{*}$ are $(t^{a})_{\smash{AB}\vphantom{\beta}}=(t^{a})_{\smash{[AB]}\vphantom{\beta}}$ . These are normalized according to

$$ \displaystyle\delta^{a}{}_{b}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{b})^{AB}\qquad\resizebox{}{}{\scalebox{0.95}[0.95]{{\hbox{{\text{and}}}}}}\qquad(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{CD}=2\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{[A}{}_{C}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{B]}{}_{D}\,. $$

Accordingly, raised and lowered adjoint indices are related to fundamental indices by

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}X^{AB}=(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}&\,,\quad X^{a}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{AB}\,,\\
Y_{AB}=Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}&\,,\quad Y_{a}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006ptY_{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{AB}\,.\end{split} $$

Note that the pairing between $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(4)^{*}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006ptY_{AB}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{AB}\,. $$

Finally, the structure constants are

$$ \displaystyle(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006ptf^{a}{}_{bc}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{1}^{b}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{2}^{c}=X_{1}^{AC}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{CD}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{2}^{DB}-X_{2}^{AC}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{CD}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{1}^{DB}\,, $$

when expressed in the adjoint and fundamental representations.

Interestingly, two metrics can be endowed to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ . Firstly, we have the usual positive-definite Killing form that universally exists in any dimensions:

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{ab}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{AC}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{BD}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{b})^{CD}\,,\quad\delta^{ab}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{b})_{CD}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{AC}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{BD}\,,\quad\delta^{ac}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{cb}=\delta^{a}{}_{b}\,. $$

Indices are raised and lowered with this metric, which is consistent with the usual practice of raising and lowering fundamental indices with the flat Euclidean metric.

On the other hand, there is also a metric specific to four dimensions:

$$ \displaystyle\textstyle{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}_{ab}=\frac{1}{4}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{ABCD}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{b})^{CD}\,,\quad{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ab}=\frac{1}{4}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{b})_{CD}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon^{ABCD}\,,\quad{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ac}\hskip 0.50003pt{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}_{cb}=\delta^{a}{}_{b}\,. $$

Evidently, this implements the Hodge dual. For instance,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}({\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}_{ab}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{b})\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{AB}&={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{ABCD}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{CD}={\star X}_{AB}\,,\\
(t_{a})^{AB}\hskip 1.00006pt({\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ab}Y_{b})&={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon^{ABCD}\hskip 1.00006ptY_{CD}={\star Y}^{AB}\,.\end{split} $$

Note that this metric naturally appears in the Palatini Lagrangian in Eq. (52).2424 24 In fact, Plebański gravity without the Immirzi constant can be described solely in terms of this split-signature Killing form. It has $(3,3)$ split signature, which connects to the decomposition $\mathfrak{so}(4)\cong\mathfrak{su}(2){\hskip 1.00006pt\oplus\,}\mathfrak{su}(2)$ . Note also the identities

$$ \displaystyle{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ad}\delta_{dc}\hskip 1.00006pt{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ce}\delta_{eb}=\delta^{a}{}_{b}\,,\quad f^{a}{}_{bc}\hskip 1.00006pt{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{be}\hskip 0.50003pt{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{cf}=f^{a}{}_{bc}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{be}\hskip 0.50003pt\delta^{cf}\,, $$

which hold because the Hodge star squares to the identity in Euclidean signature.

Next, we discuss the spinor representations. In accordance with the isomorphism $\mathfrak{so}(4)\cong\mathfrak{su}(2){\hskip 1.00006pt\oplus\,}\mathfrak{su}(2)$ , the six Lorentz generators split into two sets of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generators, which are symmetric $2{\,\times\,}2$ matrices normalized according to

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\delta^{a}{}_{b}&=(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}_{b})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}+(t^{a})_{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{b})^{\alpha\beta}\,,\\
(\tilde{t}_{a})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\gamma}}{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}&=\delta^{({\dot{\alpha}}}{}_{\smash{{\dot{\gamma}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{{\dot{\beta}})}{}_{\smash{{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\,,\quad(t_{a})^{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{\smash{\gamma\delta}\vphantom{\beta}}=\delta_{\smash{\gamma}\vphantom{\beta}}{}^{(\alpha}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{\smash{\delta}\vphantom{\beta}}{}^{\beta)}\,.\end{split} $$

In accordance with the above, adjoint indices are unpacked to spinor indices as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\tilde{X}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}=(\tilde{t}_{a})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}X^{a}\,,\quad X^{a}=(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\tilde{X}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}&\,,\quad\tilde{Y}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}=Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\,,\quad Y_{a}=\tilde{Y}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}_{a})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\,,\\
X^{\alpha\beta}=(t_{a})^{\alpha\beta}X^{a}\,,\quad X^{a}=(t^{a})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{\alpha\beta}&\,,\quad Y_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}=Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{a})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\,,\quad Y_{a}=Y_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{\alpha\beta}\,.\end{split} $$

For example, it follows that

$$ \displaystyle X^{a}=(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\tilde{X}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}+(t^{a})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{\alpha\beta}\,,\quad Y_{a}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{a}=\tilde{Y}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\tilde{X}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}+Y_{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006ptX^{\alpha\beta}\,. $$

Also, the structure constants are given as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}(t_{a})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\hskip 1.00006ptf^{a}{}_{bc}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{1}^{b}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{2}^{c}&=(\tilde{X}_{1})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\gamma}}}\hskip 1.00006pt{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\gamma}}{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{X}_{2})^{{\dot{\delta}}{\dot{\beta}}}-(\tilde{X}_{2})^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\gamma}}}\hskip 1.00006pt{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\gamma}}{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{X}_{1})^{{\dot{\delta}}{\dot{\beta}}}\,,\\
(t_{a})^{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006ptf^{a}{}_{bc}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{1}^{b}\hskip 1.00006ptX_{2}^{c}&=(X_{1})^{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{\beta\delta}\hskip 1.00006pt(X_{2})^{\delta\gamma}-(X_{2})^{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{\beta\delta}\hskip 1.00006pt(X_{1})^{\delta\gamma}\,.\end{split} $$

The dotted generators describe self-dual (right-handed) rotations while the undotted generators describe anti-self-dual (left-handed) rotations:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}_{ab}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}^{b})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}=+{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\gamma}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 0.50003pt{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\beta}}{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}_{a})^{{\dot{\gamma}}{\dot{\delta}}}\,,\quad{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}_{ab}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{b})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}=-\epsilon_{\alpha\gamma}\hskip 0.50003pt\epsilon_{\beta\delta}\hskip 1.00006pt(t_{a})^{\gamma\delta}\,.\end{split} $$

In fact, self-dual and anti-self-dual projectors arise as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\tilde{t}^{b})_{\smash{{\dot{\gamma}}{\dot{\delta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt{\tilde{\epsilon}}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\gamma}}}\hskip 1.00006pt{\tilde{\epsilon}}^{{\dot{\beta}}{\dot{\delta}}}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\hskip 0.24994pt{\delta^{ab}+{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ab}}\hskip 0.50003pt)\,,\quad(t^{a})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt(t^{b})_{\smash{\gamma\delta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon^{\alpha\gamma}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon^{\beta\delta}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\hskip 0.24994pt{\delta^{ab}-{\hskip 0.50003pt\star\hskip 0.12497pt}^{ab}}\hskip 0.50003pt)\,.\end{split} $$

Having stated our conventions abstractly, let us be slightly more concrete and note that the self-dual and anti-self-dual generators are

$$ \displaystyle(\tilde{t}^{AB})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt({\tilde{\epsilon}}\hskip 1.00006pt{\tilde{\sigma}}^{[A}\sigma^{B]})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\,,\quad(t^{AB})_{\alpha\beta}={\textstyle\frac{1}{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt(\sigma^{[A}{\tilde{\sigma}}^{B]}\epsilon)_{\alpha\beta}\,, $$

where an explicit representation of the Euclidean sigma matrices is given as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}v_{A}\hskip 1.00006pt(\sigma^{A})_{\alpha{\dot{\alpha}}}=\bigg({\begin{array}[]{cc}iv_{4}+v_{3}&v_{1}-iv_{2}\\
v_{1}+iv_{2}&iv_{4}-v_{3}\end{array}}\bigg)\,,\quad v_{A}\hskip 1.00006pt({\tilde{\sigma}}^{A})^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}=\bigg({\begin{array}[]{cc}iv_{4}-v_{3}&-v_{1}+iv_{2}\\
-v_{1}-iv_{2}&iv_{4}+v_{3}\end{array}}\bigg)\,,\end{split} $$

with the convention ${\tilde{\epsilon}}^{01}=\epsilon^{01}={\tilde{\epsilon}}_{10}=\epsilon_{10}=+1$ for the epsilon tensors.

Finally, we end with a demonstration of index conversions in the context of tetradic Palatini gravity. Let the spinor indices be raised and lowered as

$$ \displaystyle\psi^{\alpha}=\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta}\,,\quad\psi_{\alpha}=\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\hskip 1.00006pt\psi^{\beta}\,,\quad\tilde{\psi}^{\dot{\alpha}}={\tilde{\epsilon}}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\tilde{\psi}_{\dot{\beta}}\,,\quad\tilde{\psi}_{\dot{\alpha}}={\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\tilde{\psi}^{\dot{\beta}}\,. $$

The spin connection splits into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts as

$$ \displaystyle\omega^{a}=(\tilde{t}^{a})_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\tilde{\omega}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}+(t^{a})_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\omega^{\alpha\beta}\,. $$

The self-dual and anti-self-dual parts of the field strength are given by

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{R}^{\dot{\alpha}}{}_{\dot{\beta}}=d\tilde{\omega}^{\dot{\alpha}}{}_{\dot{\beta}}-\tilde{\omega}^{\dot{\alpha}}{}_{\dot{\gamma}}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\tilde{\omega}^{\dot{\gamma}}{}_{\dot{\beta}}\,,\quad R_{\alpha}{}^{\beta}=d\omega_{\alpha}{}^{\beta}+\omega_{\alpha}{}^{\gamma}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\omega_{\gamma}{}^{\beta}\,. $$

Meanwhile, it is convenient to convert the vector index of the tetrad to spinor indices with a customary factor of $-1/2$ , which originates from the $-2$ of $({\tilde{\sigma}}_{A})^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}\hskip 1.00006pt(\sigma^{A})_{\smash{\beta{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}=-2\hskip 1.00006pt\delta_{\smash{\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}{}^{\alpha}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta^{\dot{\alpha}}{}_{\smash{{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle e^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}=-\frac{1}{2}\hskip 1.00006pt({\tilde{\sigma}}_{A})^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}\hskip 1.00006pte^{A}\,. $$

Then the spinor components of the Plebański two-form defined in Eq. (51) are given by

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\tilde{B}^{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}=\epsilon_{\smash{\alpha\beta}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pte^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e^{{\dot{\beta}}\beta}\,,\quad B^{\alpha\beta}=-{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{\smash{{\dot{\alpha}}{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pte^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e^{{\dot{\beta}}\beta}\,.\end{split} $$

In turn, the Lagrangian four-form in Eq. (52) boils down to

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{g^{2}}\hskip 1.00006pt\Big(\hskip 1.00006pt{e^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}\hskip-0.50003pt{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e_{\smash{\alpha{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\tilde{R}^{\dot{\beta}}{}_{\dot{\alpha}}+e_{\smash{\beta{\dot{\alpha}}}\vphantom{\beta}}\hskip 0.50003pt{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e^{{\dot{\alpha}}\alpha}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}R_{\alpha}{}^{\beta}}\hskip 1.00006pt\Big)+\frac{\Lambda}{3g^{2}}\hskip 1.00006pte_{\smash{\alpha{\dot{\alpha}}}\vphantom{\beta}}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e^{{\dot{\alpha}}\beta}\hskip-0.50003pt{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e_{\smash{\beta{\dot{\beta}}}\vphantom{\beta}}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}e^{{\dot{\beta}}\alpha}\,. $$

The above expressions are consistent with the chiral symmetry operators in Eq. (68).

## Appendix B Geometry of Linking

In this appendix, we expand on the technical details of the Dirac delta form and topological numbers in general spacetime dimension. Here we will indicate the dimensionality of each manifold with a subscript. All manifolds will be assumed to be orientable.

#### Definitions

Consider a $p$ -dimensional submanifold ${\mathcal{N}}_{p}$ in a $d$ -dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}_{d}$ . We define a differential form analog of Dirac’s delta distribution as

$$ \displaystyle\int_{{\mathcal{N}}_{p}}\alpha^{(p)}\,\,\,=\,\,\int_{\mathcal{M}_{d}}\alpha^{(p)}\hskip-1.00006pt\wedge\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p})\,, $$

where $\alpha^{(p)}$ is an arbitrary smooth $p$ -form in $\mathcal{M}_{d}$ . Evidently, $\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p})$ is a differential $(d{\,-\,}p)$ -form distribution that peaks on the submanifold ${\mathcal{N}}_{p}$ while vanishing elsewhere.

More explicitly, suppose ${\mathcal{N}}_{p}$ is parameterized by coordinates $\sigma^{1},\sigma^{2},\cdots,\sigma^{p}$ as $x^{\mu}=X^{\mu}\hskip-0.50003pt(\sigma)$ , where $x^{\mu}$ denote coordinates of $\mathcal{M}_{d}$ . Then $\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{1}{(d{\,-\,}p)!}\bigg[\,{\int d^{p}\sigma\,\,\delta^{(d)}\hskip-0.50003pt(x{\,-\,}X(\sigma))\,\frac{\partial X^{\lambda_{1}}}{\partial\sigma^{1}}\cdots\frac{\partial X^{\lambda_{p}}}{\partial\sigma^{p}}}\,\bigg]\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{p}\mu_{1}\cdots\mu_{d-p}}\hskip 1.00006ptdx^{\mu_{1}}{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\cdots{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}dx^{\mu_{d-p}}\,,\end{split} $$

where $\delta^{(d)}\hskip-0.50003pt(x{\,-\,}X(\sigma))$ is the ordinary Dirac delta function. This is higher-form generalization of Dirac delta function will be referred to as a “Dirac delta form.” The ordinary Dirac delta corresponds to $p=0$ . It is also interesting to note that $\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{d})$ for a top-dimensional submanifold ${\mathcal{N}}_{d}$ is its characteristic function, e.g., $\delta({\mathcal{M}}_{d})=1$ .

*Figure 12: Linking between two submanifolds in $d$ dimensions.*

In terms of Dirac delta forms, the intersection number between two orientable submanifolds ${\mathcal{N}}_{p}$ and ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ in ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}$ can be defined in a coordinate-free fashion:

$$ \displaystyle\Intersect({\mathcal{N}}_{p},{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})\,=\int_{{\mathcal{M}}_{d}}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p}){\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})\,. $$

Note that the integrand $\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p}){\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})$ is a top form that localizes at the intersection points. In fact, it could be argued that $\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p}){\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})=\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p}{\,\cap\,}{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})$ . It is instructive to check if Eq. (150) defines the intersection number in an expected way with specific values of $p$ and $d$ , such as $p=0$ , or $d=3$ . Also, it is easy to see that

$$ \displaystyle\Intersect({\mathcal{N}}_{p},{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})=(-1)^{p(d-p)}\,\Intersect({\mathcal{N}}_{d-p},{\mathcal{N}}_{p})\,. $$

Given Eq. (150), we can easily define the linking number between two closed orientable submanifolds ${\mathcal{C}}_{p}$ and ${\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1}$ provided that one of them is exact. Without loss of generality, suppose $\mathcal{C}_{p}=\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1}$ . Then we define

$$ \displaystyle\Link_{*}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1},{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\,=\,\Intersect({\mathcal{N}}_{p+1},{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\,=\int_{{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1}}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})\,, $$

which counts how many times ${\mathcal{C}}_{d-p}$ penetrates the coboundary ${\mathcal{N}}_{p+1}$ as depicted in Fig. 12.

Note that the above definition necessarily puts the two arguments of $\Link_{*}$ in an unequal footing: the first argument must be exact. However, as practiced in the main text, it can be convenient to use a more handy notation for the linking number such that the exact argument can be placed in any slot. With hindsight, we define such a notation “ $\Link$ ” to satisfy the following relations:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\Link(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})&=\Link_{*}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})\,,\\
\Link({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})&=(-1)^{dp+1}\hskip 1.00006pt\Link({\mathcal{C}}_{p},{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\,.\end{split} $$

The first equation states that $\Link$ and $\Link_{*}$ give the same number when the first argument is exact. The second equation allows the arguments of $\Link$ to be freely rearranged, given the implicit assumption that one of the arguments is exact. The factor $(-1)^{dp+1}$ is necessitated from consistency with Eq. (156). Note also that the following holds:

$$ \displaystyle\Link({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1}) \displaystyle=(-1)^{d-p}\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})\,. $$

#### Identities

Using either the coordinate-free/axiomatic definition of the Dirac delta form in Eq. (148) or the explicit definition in Eq. (149), one can derive various identities of Dirac delta forms and also intersection and linking numbers. Some simple ones are

$$ \displaystyle d\hskip 1.00006pt\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{p}) \displaystyle=(-1)^{p}\,\delta(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p})\,, \displaystyle\Link(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1},\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}) \displaystyle=(-1)^{dp+1}\hskip 1.00006pt\Link(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p},\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})\,. $$

The first identity encodes Stokes theorem, while the second identity describes a duality in the linking number computation.

A few more identities are found in the context of Hamiltonian formalism. Suppose the spacetime is a product manifold ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}={\mathcal{X}}_{d-1}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\,}\mathbb{R}$ with coordinates $x^{\mu}=(x^{i},t)$ , where the last2525 25 This matches the convention chosen in Eq. (148) where the Dirac delta form is appended from the right. coordinate $x^{\mu=d}{\,=\,}t$ labels hypersurfaces foliating ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}$ . Then we consider submanifolds ${\mathcal{K}}_{p}$ and ${\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}$ of ${\mathcal{X}}_{d-1}$ that can possibly intersect, with the former being closed: $\partial{\mathcal{K}}_{p}=0$ . The corresponding relevant objects in spacetime are ${\mathcal{C}}_{p}$ and ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ , defined as the following. First, we consider an embedding of the closed submanifold ${\mathcal{K}}_{p}$ in ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}$ :

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{C}}_{p}={\mathcal{K}}_{p}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\hskip 1.00006pt}\{t_{0}\}\,. $$

Second, we consider a timelike $(d{\,-\,}p)$ -dimensional submanifold ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ of ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}$ defined as the following, where $\mathcal{I}=[t_{-},t_{+}]$ is an interval in $\mathbb{R}$ such that $t_{-}<t_{0}<t_{+}$ :

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-p}\hskip 1.00006pt{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}={\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\hskip 1.00006pt}\mathcal{I}\,. $$

The customary orientation of ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ by a sign factor $(-1)^{d-p}$ stipulates that its boundary is given in the form

$$ \displaystyle\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}\,=\,\Big(\hskip 0.50003pt{-{\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\hskip 1.00006pt}\{t_{+}\}}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big){\hskip 1.00006pt\,\cup\,\hskip 1.00006pt}\Big(\,{{\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\hskip 1.00006pt}\{t_{-}\}}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big){\hskip 1.00006pt\,\cup\,\hskip 1.00006pt}\hskip 1.00006pt\Gamma\,, $$

for a timelike submanifold $\Gamma$ in ${\mathcal{M}}_{d}$ . Specifically, the consistency between Eqs. (158) and (159) can be established by considering the Stokes theorem relating ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ and $\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ , where a factor of $(-1)^{d-p-1}$ arising from rearranging the order of the time differential $dt$ combines with the minus sign in Eq. (159) to give $(-1)^{d-p}$ .

With these definitions, it eventually follows that

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{d-p}\hskip 1.00006pt\Link(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})\hskip 1.00006pt=\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}{\hskip 1.00006pt\times\hskip 1.00006pt}\mathcal{I},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})\hskip 1.00006pt=\hskip 1.00006pt(-1)^{p}\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{K}}_{p})\,, $$

where $\Intersect_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{K}}_{p})$ is the intersection number between ${\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}$ and ${\mathcal{K}}_{p}$ in ${\mathcal{X}}_{d-1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Intersect_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{K}}_{p})\,\,=\hskip 1.00006pt\int_{{\mathcal{X}}_{d-1}}\delta_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}){\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta_{d-1}({\mathcal{K}}_{p})\,. $$

To derive Eq. (160), one may work in component terms with Eq. (149). One will find that the factor of $(-1)^{p}$ arises from an index rearrangement,

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{i_{1}\cdots i_{d-p-1}d\hskip 0.81949ptj_{1}\cdots j_{p}}=(-1)^{p}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{i_{1}\cdots i_{d-p-1}j_{1}\cdots j_{p}d}=(-1)^{p}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon_{i_{1}\cdots i_{d-p-1}j_{1}\cdots j_{p}}\,, $$

where we work with the convention such that $\epsilon_{12\cdots d}=+1$ .

#### Example: Abelian p-Form Symmetry in d Dimensions

Having derived various sign factors, we can describe a universal sign convention for higher-form symmetries of general rank $p$ in Euclidean signature spacetimes of general $d$ dimensions. Let us take an abelian $BF$ theory as a prototypical model,2626 26 For example, it is an amusing check to consider the case of $d{\,=\,}1$ , $p{\,=\,}0$ with a Lagrangian one-form $P\hskip 1.00006ptdX-H(P)\hskip 1.00006ptdt$ , which describes a point particle. In particular, it readily follows that operators $U_{\epsilon}([t_{1},t_{2}])=e^{-\epsilon\hskip 0.40974ptP(t_{2})}\hskip 0.50003pte^{\epsilon\hskip 0.40974ptP(t_{1})}$ and $Q(t)=P(t)$ implement translations of $X$ , so for example $e^{-\epsilon P}\hskip 0.24994ptX\hskip 1.00006pte^{\epsilon P}=X+\epsilon$ . whose action reads

$$ \displaystyle S\,\,=\int_{{\mathcal{M}}_{d}}B^{(d-p-1)}\hskip-1.00006pt{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}F^{(p+1)}+f(B^{(d-p-1)})\,, $$

where $F^{(p+1)}=dA^{(p)}$ . Here the superscripts denote the ranks, while $f(B^{(d-p-1)})$ is a $d$ -form functional of $B^{(d-p-1)}$ .

First, let us describe the $p$ -form symmetry in the covariant formalism. For simplicity, consider the Wilson loop for an exact support:

$$ \displaystyle W_{q}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 0.50003pt{q\int_{{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1}}F^{(p+1)}}\bigg)\,. $$

We want this to be transformed as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}W_{q}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})\hskip 1.00006pt\,\,\mapsto\,\,\,\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\Big(\hskip 1.00006pt{q\varepsilon\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big)\,W_{q}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})\,,\end{split} $$

when the symmetry operator is inserted along an exact submanifold ${\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1}=\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ . Clearly, this can be undone by a field redefinition that shifts the field strength as $F^{(p+1)}\mapsto F^{(p+1)}-\varepsilon\,\delta({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})$ ,2727 27 Concretely, from Eq. (155) it can be realized as $A^{(p)}\mapsto A^{(p)}-(-1)^{d-p}\hskip 1.00006pt\epsilon\,\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{d-p})$ , $B^{(d-p-1)}\mapsto B^{(d-p-1)}$ . which, in turn, transforms the action in Eq. (163) as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}-S\,\,\,\mapsto\,\,-S\,+\,\varepsilon\int_{{\mathcal{M}}_{d}}\kern-1.00006ptB^{(d-p-1)}\hskip-1.00006pt{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\,,\end{split} $$

from which the symmetry operator is identified:

$$ \displaystyle U_{\varepsilon}({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 1.00006pt{\varepsilon\int_{{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1}}\kern-6.00006ptB^{(d-p-1)}}\hskip 1.00006pt\bigg)\,. $$

Namely, the symmetry operator is derived as the term that is generated from the action term in the path integral after a field transformation that pushes the symmetry charge back into the defect operator. Crucially, the $BF$ structure leverages between the both sides of the Ward identity, which reads

$$ \displaystyle\big\langle\hskip 0.50003pt{U_{\varepsilon}({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\hskip 1.00006ptW_{q}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})}\hskip 0.50003pt\big\rangle=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\Big(\hskip 1.00006pt{q\varepsilon\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big)\,\big\langle\hskip 0.50003pt{W_{q}(\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1})}\hskip 0.50003pt\big\rangle\,. $$

Finally, denoting ${\mathcal{C}}_{p}=\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{p+1}$ , we can state the Ward identity in terms of a linking number:

$$ \displaystyle\big\langle\hskip 0.50003pt{U_{\varepsilon}({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1})\hskip 1.00006ptW_{q}({\mathcal{C}}_{p})}\hskip 0.50003pt\big\rangle=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\Big(\hskip 1.00006pt{(-1)^{d-p}\hskip 1.00006ptq\varepsilon\hskip 1.00006pt\Link({\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{C}}_{p})}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big)\,\big\langle\hskip 0.50003pt{W_{q}({\mathcal{C}}_{p})}\hskip 0.50003pt\big\rangle\,, $$

which follows through using Eq. (154) (or Eqs. (151), (152), and (156) with $\Link_{*}$ ).

Note that the Ward identities in the main text are reproduced when one takes $d{\,=\,}4$ and $p{\,=\,}1$ and makes the following identifications:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{C}}_{p}\,\leftrightarrow\,{\mathcal{C}}\,,\quad{\mathcal{C}}_{d-p-1}\,\leftrightarrow\,{\mathcal{S}}\,,\quad{\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}\,\leftrightarrow\,{\mathcal{V}}\,. $$

Next, we can also double check from the angle of Hamiltonian formalism. Eq. (159) as a convetion for pancaking the coboundary ${\mathcal{N}}_{d-p}$ of the symmetry operator down to a submanifold ${\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}$ in ${\mathcal{X}}_{d-1}$ stipulates that the Ward identity in Eq. (169) boils down to a conjugation of the defect operator as

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\varepsilon Q({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1})}\,W_{q}({\mathcal{K}}_{p})\,e^{\varepsilon Q({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1})}=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\Big(\hskip 1.00006pt{(-1)^{p}\hskip 1.00006ptq\varepsilon\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1},{\mathcal{K}}_{p})}\hskip 0.50003pt\Big)\,W_{q}({\mathcal{C}}_{p})\,, $$

provided that the charge operator is defined as

$$ \displaystyle Q({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1})=\int_{{\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}}\kern-6.00006ptB^{(d-p-1)} $$

as an object that lives in the $d{\,-\,}1$ dimensions. Note that the identity in Eq. (160) has been used to deduce Eq. (171) from Eq. (169). It is straightforward to verify Eq. (171) from the canonical commutation relations:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}[A_{i_{1}\cdots i_{p}},B_{k_{1}\cdots k_{d-p-1}}]\,\epsilon^{k_{1}\cdots k_{d-p-1}j_{1}\cdots j_{p}}\hskip 1.00006pt&=\hskip 1.00006pt(d{\,-\,}p{\,-\,}1)!\hskip 1.00006ptp!\hskip 1.00006pt(-1)^{p}\,\delta^{j_{1}}{}_{\smash{[i_{1}}\vphantom{\beta}}{\cdots\,}\delta^{j_{p}}{}_{\smash{i_{p}]}\vphantom{\beta}}\,,\\
{{\implies}\quad}[A_{i_{1}\cdots i_{p}},Q({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1})]\hskip 1.00006pt&=\hskip 1.00006pt(-1)^{p}\hskip 1.00006pt(\delta_{d-1}({\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}))_{i_{1}\cdots i_{p}}\,,\end{split} $$

where the factor $(-1)^{p}$ precisely arises from the same index rearrangement as in Eq. (162), provided the conventions $\epsilon_{12\cdots d}=+1$ and $t=x^{d}$ .

The above discussion corresponds to the calculation carried out in Secs. 2.2.2 and 3.2.2, so one can check consistency by taking $d{\,=\,}4$ and $p{\,=\,}1$ . Yet, note that the spatial surface “ ${\mathcal{S}}_{0}$ ” there corresponds to ${\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}$ here with a flip of orientation:

$$ \displaystyle{\mathcal{K}}_{p}\,\leftrightarrow\,{\mathcal{C}}\,,\quad{\mathcal{Y}}_{d-p-1}\,\leftrightarrow\,-{\mathcal{S}}_{0}\,. $$

This single flip is because the main text attempts to avoid any possible distractions from convention-dependent minus signs.

#### Proof of Equivalence between Eqs. (8) and (15)

Before ending, we should show that Eqs. (8) and (15), used in the main text, are equivalent statements. In $d$ -dimensional spacetime, the claim reads

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}&\lim_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\pm}\to\,{\mathcal{P}}}\hskip 0.50003pt\Omega({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+})\hskip 1.00006pt\Omega^{-1}\hskip-0.50003pt({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-})={\alpha}\in Z(G)\\
&\iff\quad\exists\,\lambda^{a}\qquad\resizebox{}{}{\scalebox{0.95}[0.95]{{\hbox{{\text{s.t.}}}}}}\qquad(\Omega^{-1}dd\Omega)^{a}=\lambda^{a}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta({\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}})\qquad\resizebox{}{}{\scalebox{0.95}[0.95]{{\hbox{{\text{and}}}}}}\qquad e^{2\pi\lambda}=\smash{{\alpha}^{(-1)^{d}}}\,,\end{split} $$

where ${\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+}$ and ${\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-}$ are points infinitesimally deviating from a point on ${\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}$ from above and below. The notion of above and below is well-defined, as ${\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}$ is oriented and codimension one. As shown below, the identities stated in Eqs. (151) and (156) play a role in the proof.

First of all, the fact that $\Omega$ as a multivalued function is everywhere smooth off the surface $\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}$ implies that $dd\Omega$ localizes on $\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}$ and vice versa, which is in turn equivalent to the existence of an algebra-valued zero-form $\lambda^{a}$ such that $(\Omega^{-1}dd\Omega)^{a}=2\pi\lambda^{a}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta({\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}})$ .

*Figure 13: The center periodicity condition on the multivalued group parameter $\Omega$ , in terms of the discontinuity $\lim_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\pm}\to\,{\mathcal{P}}}\hskip 0.50003pt(\hskip 0.12497pt\hskip 1.00006pt{\Omega({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+})\hskip 1.00006pt\Omega^{-1}\hskip-0.50003pt({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-})}\hskip 0.50003pt)={\alpha}$ across a branch cut ${\mathcal{V}}$ .*

Thus, it remains to verify that the center periodicity condition on $\Omega$ is equivalent to $e^{2\pi\lambda}={\alpha}^{(-1)^{d}}$ . It suffices to work with an exact one-dimensional loop ${\mathcal{C}}_{1}=\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{2}$ in the vicinity of $\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}$ . Suppose $\Intersect({\mathcal{V}}_{d-1},\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{2})=-1$ . Then the periodicity condition implies

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\lim_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}_{1}\to\,{\mathcal{C}}_{1}}\hskip 0.50003pt\mathrm{P}\kern-1.00006pt\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 0.50003pt{\oint_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}_{1}}\Omega^{-1}d\Omega}\bigg)=\lim_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}_{1}\to\,{\mathcal{C}}_{1}}\hskip 0.50003pt\Omega^{-1}\hskip-0.50003pt({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-})\hskip 1.00006pt\Omega({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+})=\alpha\,,\end{split} $$

where ${\mathcal{C}}^{\prime}_{1}$ is the infinitesimal opening of ${\mathcal{C}}_{1}$ described before. Meanwhile, the left-hand side can be computed as a surface-ordered integral, thanks to the nonabelian Stokes theorem:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{P}\kern-1.00006pt\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 0.50003pt{\oint_{\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{2}}\Omega^{-1}d\Omega}\bigg)=\mathrm{P}\kern-1.00006pt\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 0.50003pt{\int_{{\mathcal{N}}_{2}}\Omega^{-1}dd\Omega}\bigg) \displaystyle=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\bigg(\hskip 0.50003pt{\int_{{\mathcal{M}}_{d}}\Omega^{-1}dd\Omega{\hskip 1.00006pt{\wedge}\,}\delta({\mathcal{N}}_{2})}\bigg)\,. $$

Note that the last equality has dropped the surface ordering because the integrand localizes at a single point. Plugging in $(\Omega^{-1}dd\Omega)^{a}=2\pi\lambda^{a}\hskip 1.00006pt\delta({\partial{\mathcal{V}}})$ , the right-hand side boils down to $\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\,(2\pi\lambda\hskip 1.00006pt\Intersect(\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1},{\mathcal{N}}_{2}))$ , which equals $\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\,((-1)^{d}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda)$ given $\Intersect({\mathcal{V}}_{d-1},\partial{\mathcal{N}}_{2})=-1$ by Eqs. (151) and (156). Therefore, demanding that the outcomes of Eqs. (176) and (177) are the same, we find $\alpha=\exp\hskip-1.00006pt\,((-1)^{d}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda)$ , i.e., $e^{2\pi\lambda}={\alpha}^{(-1)^{d}}$ . Lastly, recalling the fact that ${\alpha}{\,\in\,}Z(G)$ , it can be seen that supposing generic curves with arbitrary linking numbers does not impose a further condition on $\lambda^{a}$ . This concludes the proof.

To make it certain that all the signs have worked properly, it is instructive to double check by considering the abelian version of the statement:

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{{\mathcal{P}}_{\pm}\to\,{\mathcal{P}}}\hskip 0.50003pt\chi({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+}){\,-\,}\chi({\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-})=(-1)^{d}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda\quad\iff\quad dd\chi=2\pi\lambda\,\delta({\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1}})\,. $$

Here $\lambda$ is a constant. The periodicity condition in the left-hand side is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle d\chi+(-1)^{d}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda\,\delta({\mathcal{V}}_{d-1})=df\,, $$

for some single-valued zero-form $f$ ; i.e., $d\chi$ is “gauge equivalent” to $(-1)^{d-1}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda\,\delta({\mathcal{V}}_{d-1})$ . Thus it follows that $dd\chi=(-1)^{d-1}\hskip 1.00006pt2\pi\lambda\,d\hskip 1.00006pt\delta({\mathcal{V}}_{d-1})$ , which equals $2\pi\lambda\,\delta(\partial{\mathcal{V}}_{d-1})$ by Eq. (155).

Note that the points ${\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt+}$ and ${\mathcal{P}}_{\hskip-0.40974pt-}$ in Fig. 2 are correctly deviating from above and below as stated in Eq. (175) ( $-\Link({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{S}})=\Link({\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{C}})=\Intersect({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{C}})=-1$ ), but the three-dimensional visualization seemingly appears the opposite due to the relative orientation with the hidden fourth dimension.

# Nonperturbative Double Copy in Flatland

Clifford Cheung ,1 James Mangan ,2 Julio Parra-Martinez ,1 and Nabha Shah 1

1Walter Burke Institute for Theoretical Physics, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA 2Department of Physics and Astronomy, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208, USA

(Received 14 May 2022; revised 17 August 2022; accepted 3 October 2022; published 23 November 2022)

We derive a nonperturbative, Lagrangian-level formulation of the double copy in two spacetime dimensions. Our results elucidate the field theoretic underpinnings of the double copy in a broad class of scalar theories which can include masses and higher-dimension operators. An immediate corollary is the amplitudes-level double copy at all orders in perturbation theory. Applied to certain integrable models, the double copy defines an isomorphism between Lax connections, Wilson lines, and infinite towers of conserved currents. We also implement the double copy at the level of nonperturbative classical solutions, both analytically and numerically, and present a generalization of the double copy map that includes a fixed tower of higher-dimension corrections given by the Moyal algebra.

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.221602

Introduction.—Recent breakthroughs in scattering theory have unveiled an extraordinary hidden structure lying dormant within the fundamental laws of nature. The so-called “double copy” [1–4] is a mathematical formula, only proven at tree level, that very simply relates perturbative scattering amplitudes of gravitons in Einstein’s general relativity (GR) to those of gluons in Yang-Mills theory (YM). At a purely practical level, the double copy is an immensely efficient tool for recycling past results in gauge theory to derive new ones for gravity. This approach has made feasible many previously intractable calculations, for example, those relevant to the finiteness of supergravity theories [5– 12] and more recently, post-Minkowskian computations for black hole binary dynamics [13–16] which are directly relevant to the LIGO experimental program [17,18] and are, within the last three years, competing with the state of the art. At the conceptual level, the double copy remains deeply mysterious. Its structure transcends gauge theory and gravity and applies to a broad web of theories [3]. For example, the exact same double copy also relates all tree-level amplitudes of pions in the chiral limit to those of certain hypothetical scalars known as Galileons, which have been studied independently as viable theories of cosmology and modified gravity. In broad strokes, the double copy maps gauge theory to gravity by first expressing every gauge theory amplitude as a sum over cubic graphs,

where the ci are color factors (structure constants), the ni are kinematic numerators, and the di are propagators [1– 3,19,20]. Color-kinematics duality states that there exists a rearrangement of terms such that the kinematic numerators obey the same Jacobi identities as the color factors. Gravity—as the square or double copy of gauge theory—is simply obtained by replacing each color factor with the associated kinematic numerator, ci →ni. The double copy is an established fact about flat space, perturbative scattering amplitudes, but its generality is far from understood. To what extent does it apply offshell [21–27]? To curved geometries [28–38]? Nonperturbatively? Finding answers to these questions could provide a nonperturbative, background independent mapping between gravity and far simpler quantum field theories. In this Letter, we present a nonperturbative double copy in two spacetime dimensions. This is the first offshell Lagrangian level formulation of the double copy for interacting theories. [39]. Extending the proof of the double copy from tree level to all loop orders has implications for the understanding of all double copy constructions. Integrable models.—Since ZM theory is classically equivalent to the PCM, it is similarly integrable [41,52,62]. Moreover, ZM theory maps to the SG under the double copy, so we will see that the latter is also integrable. Note that mapping the integrability of one theory to another would not be possible with the standard amplitudes-level double copy because the integrability conditions are expressed in terms of currents and off-shell fields. As a brief review, integrability is achieved by casting the equations of motion into the form of the Lax equation, _L ¼ ½M; L, where the operators L and M constitute a Lax pair [63–67]. By virtue of this form of the equations of motion, the eigenvalues of L are conserved charges. A familiar Lax pair is the Hamiltonian together with an observable in the Heisenberg picture. In two dimensions, integrability requires infinitely many charges where the infinitude of Lax pairs is parameterized by a spectral parameter λ. The Lax pair comes from a Wilson line and a gauge field, the Lax connection, where flatness of the gauge connection yields the Lax equation. On the other hand, a generic gauge theory amplitude with arbitrary color structures will not have any interpretation as a gravity amplitude. That the SG is secretly free certainly detracts from the miracle of a nonperturbative mapping in this context.

[49]. Future directions.—The double copy is an extremely potent computational tool but it is fundamentally unclear why it works. Our results mark a radical departure from the status quo of the double copy in several ways. Typical theories that admit color-kinematics duality have a single coupling constant, massless particles, square in any spacetime dimension, only double copy on-shell, and all of this is only provable at tree level [3]. On the other hand we have presented an enormous class of scalar theories with arbitrary Wilson coefficients and masses that square off-shell (to all orders in perturbation theory) in two dimensions. A Lagrangian formulation coupled with an understanding of the algebra mapping also broadens the scope of the double copy to include Wilson lines, currents, and nonperturbative (non-Abelian) classical solutions. The present Letter leaves several avenues for further inquiry. In general dimensions, the kinematic algebra for the NLSM is that of volume-preserving diffeomorphisms [24]. Generalizing this tree-level observation to the full loop-level action is an open problem. The two-dimensional results presented here suggest that this generalization may be possible, at least in principle. While we have found an enormous class of operators that double copy, it may be possible to enlarge the space even further by overcoming the restrictions (i) and (ii) given above. Finally, it would also be interesting to apply our approach to gauge theory and gravity in two dimensions and beyond. The kinematic algebra for gauge theory [24], even at tree level, is not as well understood as for the NLSM. However, the self-dual sector of Yang-Mills theory has a simple kinematic algebra so it may be possible to systematically perturb away from the self-dual sector [21,22].
